API clients: personal keys and OAuth clients with their scopes. A program calls the API with one of two kinds of credential: API key ( osk_… ), sent as a bearer token. Good for scripts. OAuth client : a client id and secret exchanged at /api/v1/oauth/token (client-credentials grant) for a one-hour access token signed by the server. Good for services; the keys that verify tokens are at /.well-known/jwks.json . Each client gets only the scopes it needs and an expiry between 1 and 3,650 days. OpenSeal is a deterministic, headless agreement engine in Rust, hosted by a server of record. The engine owns the PDF, the fields, the routing rules, the seal and the evidence. The server owns identity, storage, delivery, keys and policy. Every arrow leaving the deployment goes through a host seam; the engine knows none of them exist.

OpenSeal's sister projects, OpenCalc and OpenPresent, are document editors where the file is the product and a server only orders edits. In an e-signature product the product is the evidence that the file was agreed to , no party may hold the only copy of it, and no party trusts another. So the engine-and-host split is kept, and the server becomes the system of record.

Pure Rust crates that compile unchanged to native code and to WebAssembly. Time, randomness, keys, fonts, trust lists and network answers are supplied as values, so the same input gives the same bytes and every verdict is the same on every host. Both server and worker change an envelope only by applying a typed command through the workflow engine, which returns the new state, the audit events and the effects to perform. The audit events are committed in the same transaction

Upload, admit (bounded parse, active content removed, a report), store the original and its hash, prepare recipients and fields, validate, send. The document hash is fixed and the first recipients are invited.
The link, authentication, consent, the exact bytes whose hash is in the chain, fields validated by the engine in the browser and again on the server, adopt, review, finish. The workflow advances.

The last action moves the envelope to completing . The worker flattens values, adds the certificate and the audit trail, has keyd sign the digest, timestamps it, optionally adds long-term validation data, verifies the result, stores it and records envelope.completed with the sealed hash.
Anyone with the PDF runs the same verifier in the browser or on the command line, against the roots they trust. No server is involved.

Plain ES modules with no framework and no bundler, as in the sister projects, under a strict Content Security Policy. PDF pages are drawn by pdf.js in a worker with scripting disabled. It is one client of the public API: everything it does, an integrator can do too. The full design is in docs/02, the high-level design .

OpenSeal is built in the open, and contributions are welcome. Because evidence integrity is the product's most critical property, the bar for changes that read, write or sign a PDF is high, and every rule below has a reason.

h: Are signatures made with OpenSeal legally binding?
t: OpenSeal is designed to support electronic-signature laws such as ESIGN and UETA in the United States and eIDAS in the European Union. Whether a particular signature is valid depends on the deployment, its configuration, the jurisdiction and the transaction. Nothing on this site is legal advice; ask counsel for your case.

h: Is it certified for SOC 2, ISO 27001 or 21 CFR Part 11?
t: No. A self-hosted deployment is certified by its operator, not by the software. OpenSeal plans control mappings to help operators ( LEG-04 ) and a Part 11 mode ( VS-19 ); neither is a certification.

h: Does it support qualified electronic signatures (QES)?
t: Not yet. Remote signing through a qualified trust service provider with the CSC API is planned ( VS-18 ).

h: Can I use OpenSeal in a commercial or closed-source product?
t: Yes. It is licensed under Apache-2.0: you may use, modify, embed, host and sell products built with it, with no royalties and no separate commercial licence. When you redistribute it, keep the LICENSE and the NOTICE file. See brand and attribution .

h: Do I have to show "Powered by OpenSeal"?
t: No. It is appreciated, never required, and OpenSeal never adds it to your application or your PDFs.

h: Why not use an existing open-source project?
t: The established open-source e-signature projects (DocuSeal, Documenso, OpenSign by OpenSign Labs, LibreSign) are licensed under the AGPL, which many companies cannot ship inside their products, and several keep features such as conditional fields, bulk send or SSO in paid editions. OpenSeal is permissively licensed and plans every feature for the open core. OpenSeal is written clean-room: no code from those projects is copied or adapted.

h: How can someone check a document without OpenSeal?
t: The sealed PDF is standard PAdES, so independent validators such as pyHanko and EU DSS check it, and OpenSeal's own verifier runs offline in a browser or on the command line. See Verifying a document .

h: What happens if the OpenSeal server disappears?
t: Every party already holds the sealed PDF with its certificate of completion and audit trail inside, protected by the seal and a trusted timestamp. Nothing needs the server to be verified.

h: Where are the signing keys kept?
t: In keyd, a separate service that uses your HSM through PKCS#11 and signs digests only. See Signing keys .

Yes: a REST API under /api/v1 , described in OpenAPI, with API keys and OAuth client credentials, idempotency keys, ETags for safe concurrent edits, and signed webhooks. See the API reference and Webhooks .

h: Is the API compatible with DocuSign's?
t: Its concepts are the familiar ones (envelopes, recipients, routing orders, fields, templates, embedded views). A DocuSign-shaped compatibility endpoint is a separate, later question, to be decided with counsel ( VS-25 ).

h: Can I embed signing in my application?
t: An embedded signing link for a recipient is available through the API today. Embeddable signing and preparing elements are planned ( VS-09 ).

The product is not the PDF; it is the proof that the PDF was agreed to. A completed agreement must show which document every party saw, who signed it, when and how, and anyone must be able to check that offline for decades. This page explains how, and what is still to be reviewed. OpenSeal is designed to support electronic-signature laws such as ESIGN, UETA and eIDAS. It makes no claim of legal validity, compliance or certification. An external security and cryptographic review ( SEC-REV-01 ) and an ASVS self-assessment are release gates still ahead. Report vulnerabilities privately: see the s

Nobody in an agreement trusts anybody else, so the design assumes each of them may attack the record: a signer who later says "I never signed", or tries to change the document after signing; a sender who wants a signer to agree to something other than what they saw; a counterparty holding the PDF who alters it while keeping a valid look (shadow and incremental-saving attacks); another tenant on the same install, an outside attacker , a malicious integrator abusing webhooks or embedded views; an insider or compromised operator who would rewrite evidence, backdate, or sign with the platform key.

Like DocuSign and SignNow by default, OpenSeal separates the person's electronic signature (a typed, drawn or uploaded mark adopted with intent, plus the evidence of who adopted it) from the platform's digital signature , the seal: a cryptographic signature over the final bytes that proves the record has not changed since. Signatures made with each signer's own certificate, for advanced and qualified signatures, are planned ( VS-18 ).

PAdES baseline profiles. B-T is the default: a CAdES-detached CMS signature with an RFC 3161 timestamp from a timestamp authority, so the time does not come from our clock. B-LT adds the certificates and revocation data needed to validate years later without a network; B-LTA adds a document timestamp over everything, renewed before algorithms or certificates weaken. Incremental, never rewritten. The sealed file starts with the exact bytes delivered to signers. Anything later, such as long-term validation data, is appended as a new revision. Every legally relevant fact is an event , written in the same database transaction as the change it describes, before the client hears success. Append-only. No code path updates or deletes an event; the application's database role cannot, and a trigger refuses it. Corrections are new events. Hash-chained per envelope. Each event is canonical JSON (RFC 8785) whose SHA-256 is the next event's prev ; sequence numbers are dense. Removing, inserting, reordering or editing any event breaks the chain. Sealed into the document. The chain is embedded in the sealed PDF as audit-trail.json , and the cert

Appended to the sealed PDF: the envelope summary and chain head; each document's SHA-256 as delivered; for each signer, their email (masked as the account chooses), authentication methods and results, IP address, user agent, location and how it was obtained, the signature images and adoption method, and the sent, viewed and signed times; consent versions and times; and how to verify. See an example .

The seal key lives in keyd , a separate daemon that talks PKCS#11 to an HSM (SoftHSM in development). It receives the encoded signed attributes, never the document, and returns the signature. keyd accepts only the worker, over TLS 1.3 with mutual authentication and a client allow-list, rate-limits requests, and keeps its own hash-chained log of every operation. File keys are refused outside development, and any seal made with one says so in its reason. No private key appears in code, logs, the database or an image. Cloud KMS backends (AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault) are planned ( KEYD-01 ).

Every uploaded file is assumed to be an attack. The PDF reader is OpenSeal's own: every limit (size, depth, object count, stream expansion and more) is named, has an error code, a hostile test file and a fuzz target, and each target has been fuzzed for 24 cumulative hours without a finding. Uploads are rewritten into a fresh file without JavaScript, launch actions, embedded files, external references or XFA, which are never executed or followed; what was removed is reported to the sender. The browser draws pages with pdf.js with scripting disabled, inside a strict Content Security Policy.

Our verifier is not trusted alone. Every sealed and every tampered fixture must get the same verdict from three validators: casual-sign-verify , pyHanko and EU DSS. Across a corpus of 422 real-world PDFs, all 417 admissible files are filled, flattened, sealed and verified by all three. The verifier's classifier of later revisions catches shadow attacks (hide, replace, hide-and-replace) and incremental-saving attacks. The same verifier compiled to WebAssembly gives byte-identical verdicts in the browser.

Access is decided on the server for every request and every object, deny by default. PostgreSQL row-level security per account is a second line, not the first; isolation tests are generated from the API description and run with it on and off. Another account's objects answer exactly like missing ones. Signing links are opaque, for one recipient of one envelope, and bound to the first browser that opens them; they are never logged. Signers need no account. They follow the link in their invitation, on a phone or a computer, and the page guides them through every field.

Open the link. Each link is for one recipient of one envelope. It is bound to the browser that opens it first. Prove who you are , when the sender asked for it: an access code shared outside the email. Share your location , if you choose. The browser asks; declining is fine, and the certificate then records an approximate location from the network address, saying so. Consent to electronic records. The signer reads the disclosure and agrees to use electronic records and signatures. The version they accepted is recorded. Fill the fields. Start jumps to the first required field and Next to the on

The name is filled in and can be edited. A signer can type it and pick one of the script styles, draw it with a mouse, finger or pen, or upload an image. By choosing Adopt and sign they agree that the mark is their electronic signature for these documents. The script fonts shown on screen are the same files the engine embeds in the sealed PDF. On a phone, the panel rises from the bottom. Pages fit the width; targets are at least 44 pixels.

The last signer sees a confirmation. The worker then flattens every value into the documents, adds the certificate of completion and the audit trail, seals the result and checks the seal before releasing it. Recipients are emailed when the sealed document is ready. The confirmation after finishing.

The signing page is designed for WCAG 2.2 AA: every field is reachable with Tab in reading order, required fields are named as required, the field list is an alternative to the page, typing a signature is the default, and text and controls meet contrast minimums in light and dark themes. A template saves what stays the same from one envelope to the next: documents, roles in routing order, the fields each role fills, and the email subject and message. When you use it, you only name the people.

A template has roles such as "Employee" or "Company signer" instead of names and email addresses. Each role has a type (signer or carbon copy) and a routing order, and fields belong to roles. Using the template asks for one person per role. Templates, ready to use.

Open Templates and choose New template . Name it and add its documents. They are admitted and cleaned like any upload. Add the roles in routing order. Place fields for each role, as in the editor . Save. Edits later change the template only; envelopes already sent from it keep their own copies.

Choose Use next to a template, fill in a name and email for each role, adjust the message if you like, and send. You can also duplicate a template to start a variant, or delete one; envelopes made from it are not affected.

A completed agreement carries its own proof. Anyone holding the sealed PDF can check it, with no account and without asking the server that made it.

The seal : the byte ranges it covers, the digest, the CMS signature, and the certificate chain up to a root you trust. The timestamp : when the seal was made, from an RFC 3161 timestamp authority rather than the server's clock. Every later revision : anything appended after the seal must be of a kind the seal allows (for example long-term validation data). Anything else, including the hiding and replacing tricks known as shadow attacks, makes the document fail. The audit trail embedded as audit-trail.json : every event's hash, its link to the one before, and the sequence.

Open /verify.html on any OpenSeal install, or serve the web app yourself. Drop the PDF on the page. The check is the engine's own verifier compiled to WebAssembly: it runs in your browser and the file is never uploaded. A sealed test document, signed and unchanged. Add the certificate of the authority you trust under Trusted certificates (DER or PEM): your organisation's root, or the root of the service that sealed the document. Without one, the verifier can confirm the document is unchanged but not who issued the seal, and says so.

The verify page needs nothing from a server once it has loaded: save it, or serve webapp/ from a laptop with python3 -I tools/serve-webapp.py , disconnect, and verify. The verifier module is built by tools/build-webapp-wasm.sh .

The openseal command runs the same engine natively. cargo build --release -p casual-sign-cli target/release/openseal verify agreement.pdf --trust root.pem target/release/openseal verify agreement.pdf --trust root.pem --json target/release/openseal audit verify audit-trail.json --head <chain head> Exit codes: 0 every signature passed and the last covers the whole file; 1 verification failed; 4 indeterminate (nothing failed, but not every signature could be confirmed, for example without a trusted root). openseal help lists them all.

OpenSeal seals are standard PAdES, so tools that know nothing about OpenSeal can check them. The project's own tests require three to agree on every sealed and every tampered fixture: our verifier, pyHanko and the European Commission's DSS . pip install pyhanko pyhanko sign validate --trust root.pem --pretty-print agreement.pdf Validation in Adobe Acrobat is a release gate ( PV-01 ) that has not been passed yet, so OpenSeal makes no claim about how Acrobat shows its seals. Seals from the development stack validate only against that stack's generated root.

Outcome Means Signed and unchanged Every signature checks out, and nothing changed after signing except what the signatures allow. Indeterminate Nothing failed, but something could not be confirmed: usually the issuer is not among your trusted certificates. Failed A signature does not verify, or the document was changed in a way its signatures do not allow. Treat it as altered.

OpenSeal tells your system when something happens to an envelope by POSTing a small, signed JSON event to an HTTPS endpoint you register. Events carry ids and statuses only; your system fetches the details it needs with its own credentials.

A subscription names the URL, the event types (or * for all), and references to one to four secrets. Secrets are provisioned by the operator, as an environment variable or a file the worker can read, so they never travel through the API. A secret is whsec_ followed by base64 of at least 16 random bytes. Optionally, limit the subscription to one envelope. curl https://sign.example.com/api/v1/webhooks \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENSEAL_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: crm-webhook-1" \ -d '{ "url": "https://crm.example.com/hooks/openseal", "event_types": ["enve

Events mirror the audit trail's types that matter to integrators: Envelope: envelope.sent , envelope.delivered , envelope.completing (sealing has started), envelope.completed , envelope.declined , envelope.voided , envelope.expired , envelope.corrected , envelope.purged Recipient: recipient.sent , recipient.delivered , recipient.auth_failed , recipient.completed , recipient.declined , recipient.reassigned , recipient.bounced Designed but not emitted yet: recipient.finish_later , template.* and bulk_send.completed .

{ "id": "0193a1b2-…", "type": "envelope.completed", "created_at": "2026-11-12T09:14:03Z", "account_id": "0193a1b2-…", "data": { "envelope_id": "0193a1b2-…", "status": "completed", "version": 7, "recipient_id": "0193a1b2-…" } } No names, email addresses, subjects, field values or documents are sent, so a misconfigured endpoint leaks nothing about the agreement. recipient_id appears on recipient events. Every attempt of one event sends the same bytes.

Deliveries follow the Standard Webhooks scheme. Three headers come with each request: webhook-id : the event delivery's id, the same on every retry; use it to ignore duplicates. webhook-timestamp : the attempt's Unix time; reject anything more than five minutes old. webhook-signature : v1, and the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of id.timestamp.body , once per active secret, separated by spaces (so secrets can be rotated). import base64, hashlib, hmac, time def verify(secret: str, headers: dict, body: bytes) -> bool: key = base64.b64decode(secret.removeprefix("whsec_")) msg_id, ts = headers["webhook-id"],

Any 2xx answer within 10 seconds counts as delivered. Redirects are not followed. Otherwise the worker retries with exponential back-off (from 30 seconds, doubling, capped at 12 hours, with jitter) for 15 attempts, about three days. Delivery is at least once: the same event may arrive twice with the same webhook-id . Order is not guaranteed; compare version to discard stale events.

Only https:// URLs to public addresses. Private, loopback, link-local (including cloud metadata), carrier-grade NAT, reserved and multicast addresses are refused, both when the address is resolved and again when the connection is made, so DNS rebinding cannot reach your internal network. An operator can allow a private range with OPENSEAL_WEBHOOK_ALLOW . Planned: manual redelivery, disabling a subscription that has failed for five days, filters by sender or template, and optional mutual TLS to receivers.

If you find a weakness in OpenSeal, please tell us privately first, so it can be fixed before it is used against anyone.
Do not open a public issue for a suspected vulnerability, a malicious PDF, a signature-forgery technique, or a real signed agreement.

Use GitHub private vulnerability reporting for the OpenSeal repository. Include: the affected revision (a commit id); the subsystem: PDF reader, sealing, verification, the signing ceremony, the API, or keyd; the impact and a realistic attack path; a minimal reproduction without personal data or real agreements . We will acknowledge the report, assess it, coordinate a fix and an advisory, and credit you if you wish.
Signature and evidence issues come first: a tampered document that still verifies; a seal that verifies in one validator and fails in another; an audit chain that can be altered without detection.
